column2: Having enjoyed great pleasures there, at the end, when merit is exhausted, you will experience here whatever small inauspicious fruit remains."
Those men who, by the power of merit, see that Dharmaraja, gentle-minded, like their own ancestor,
therefore dharma should always be served, giver of the fruit of liberation; from dharma are told wealth, desire and liberation.
Dharma is mother, father, brother; dharma is lord and friend; dharma is master, companion, protector, creator and nourisher.
From dharma wealth, from wealth desire, from desire enjoyment and pleasures; from dharma lordship and one-pointedness; from dharma the supreme course to heaven.
Dharma, served, Brahmins, saves from great fear; from dharma one attains godhood and Brahmin-hood, without doubt.
When men's sin accumulated earlier is exhausted, then their intellect, best of Brahmins, turns to dharma here.
One who, having obtained rare human birth after thousands of other births, does not practise dharma is surely deceived.
The despised, the poor, the ugly, the sick, servants of others and fools should be known as devoid of dharma.
Those who are long-lived, heroic, learned, enjoyers, wealthy, healthy and handsome — by them dharma was done earlier.
Thus the Brahmins devoted to dharma go to the highest goal; those who serve adharma go to animal birth.
Men devoted to Vasudeva, destroyer of hells, do not see Yama or the hells even in a dream.
Men who constantly bow to the god without beginning or end, tearer of Daityas and Danavas, do not see Yama.
Those who have taken refuge in Achyuta by deed, mind and word — Yama has no power over them; they share in the fruit of liberation.
People who constantly bow to Narayana, the lord of the worlds, Brahmins, go nowhere except to Vishnu's abode.
They see neither the messengers, nor that road, nor Yama, nor that city; having bowed to Vishnu they never see the hells.
Even men who have committed sin many times, bewildered, do not go to hell if they bow to Hari, remover of all sin.
Even those who deceitfully remember Janardana go, having given up the body, to Vishnu's faultless world.
Even one who is intensely attached to anger, if he at some time utters Hari's name, is freed with the exhaustion of faults, like the king of Chedi.
In Yama's divine palace, equal in qualities to Brahma's world, a creature bound by fixed actions experiences sorrows.
By what disposition and by what action a man goes to a terrible state I shall now tell.
A twice-born, deluded, having studied the four Vedas, then accepting gifts from a fallen person, is born in the womb of an ass.
The ass lives fifteen years, Brahmins; the ass, dead, becomes an ox and lives seven years.
The dead ox is born a Brahma-Rakshasa; after three months as Brahma-Rakshasa he is born a Brahmin.
Having officiated for a fallen person, he is born in a worm's womb; there he lives fifteen years, Brahmins.
Freed from the state of a worm, he is then born as an ass; five years as an ass, five years as a boar,
five years as a cock, five years as a jackal, one year as a dog; then he is born a human.
A foolish pupil who commits a sin against his teacher gets three births in worldly existence, no doubt.
First he becomes a dog, Brahmins, then a flesh-eater, then an ass; after death among the afflicted, afterwards he is born a Brahmin.
The sinner pupil who even in mind approaches his teacher's wife goes into severe rebirths here through unrighteousness of mind.
Born in a dog's womb he lives three years; dying there, he is born in a worm's womb.
Having become a worm he lives one year; then, on death, he is born in a Brahmin womb.
If a teacher without cause kills his pupil, who is equal to a son, by his own willfulness he too is born a violent being.
The son who disrespects his father and mother, Brahmins, that creature after death is first born an ass.
Having attained ass-hood he lives ten years; for one year a crocodile; then he is born a human.
The son whose mother and father are both angry because of his disregard for elders also, dying, is born an ass.
The ass lives ten and four months; as a cat seven months; then he is born a human.
One who abuses mother and father is born a mynah; one who has struck them, Brahmins, is born a tortoise.
The tortoise for ten years, the porcupine three years, and having been a snake six months, then he is born a human.
One who eats his master's food and serves what is hated by the king, he too, fallen into delusion, dying is born a monkey.
A monkey for ten years, a mouse for seven years, a dog six months; then he is born a human.
The man who misappropriates a deposit, gone to Yama's realm, after a hundred rebirths is born in a worm's womb.
He lives there fifteen years, Brahmins; having exhausted his evil deed, he is then born a human.
The envious man dying is born a Sharngaka bird; the betrayer of trust, the evil-minded, is born a fish.
Having been a fish eight years, he is born a deer, Brahmins; a deer four months, then he is born a goat.
The goat on death, after a full year, is born a worm; then he is born a human.
A mortal, unconscious from delusion, who steals grain, barley, sesame, black gram, horse gram, mustard, chickpeas,
peas, green gram, wheat, linseed or other crops is born, best of sages, a shameless mouse.
Then after death, best of sages, he dying is born a boar; the boar, just born, dies again of disease.
Then he is born a dumb dog; by that action the man, having been a dog five years, is then born a man.
One who has touched another's wife is born a wolf; a dog, jackal, vulture, snake, heron, crane.
The sinner who in delusion violates his brother's wife becomes a male cuckoo for a year, Brahmins.
Having violated a friend's wife, a teacher's wife or a king's wife, the lustful dying is born a boar.
A boar five years, a crane ten years, an ant three months, an insect one month.
Having passed through these rebirths he is born in a worm's womb; he lives there fourteen months in the worm's womb.
The man, having exhausted his unrighteousness, is then born a human. One who having given a maiden earlier wishes to give her a second time,
he too, Brahmins, dying, is born in a worm's womb; he lives there thirteen years, best of Brahmins.
Freed at the exhaustion of unrighteousness, he is then born a human. One who has not done the work for the gods or for the ancestors,
not satisfying the ancestors and gods, dying is born a crow; a crow for a hundred years, then he is born a cock;
he is born a snake for a month; then a human. He who disrespects his eldest brother, equal to a father,
he too, on death, is born in a heron's womb; the heron lives ten years; he is born a jivaka;
then he meets death and attains human birth. A Shudra who has gone to a Brahmin woman is born in a worm's womb;
then on death he is born a boar again; the boar, just born, dies of disease, Brahmins.
The fool is born a dog by that action, Brahmins; having been a dog, his action done, he is then born a human.
Having produced offspring there, dying he is born a mouse. The ungrateful, dying, Brahmins, goes to Yama's realm.
In Yama's realm, bound by the cruel, he suffers pain: the rod, hammer, spear, terrible fire-rod,
the terrible sword-leaf forest, the sand, the false silk-cotton tree; these and many others he meets in Yama's realm.
Having obtained terrible torments, he then goes, Brahmins, to the wheel of worldly existence and is born in a worm's womb.
He is a worm fifteen years, Brahmins; then, reaching a womb, the man dies right there.
Then the creature enters hundreds of wombs many times; having passed through very many rebirths, he is then born an animal.
Then, having experienced sorrow for many years, joined with rebirth, he is born a tortoise.
Having stolen curd, he is a crane; unprepared fish, a diver bird; the evil-minded who steals honey is born a gadfly.
Having stolen fruit or root or a cake he is an ant; having stolen beans he is born a fruit-mouse.
Having stolen rice-pudding he gets partridge-hood; having stolen a flour cake he is born a jar-owl.
The evil-minded man who steals water is born a crow; having stolen bronze, the evil-minded man is born a harita bird.
Having stolen a silver vessel he is born a pigeon; having stolen a golden vessel he is born in a worm's womb.
Having stolen leaf-wool he gets osprey-hood; having stolen silk-cocoon he is born a dancer.
Having stolen fine cloth, he is born a human as a parrot; having stolen linen he is born, dead, a swan.
Having stolen cotton he is born a heron; having stolen silk or woollen cloth, Brahmins,
having stolen linen cloth, a hare is born; having stolen powder the man is born, dead, a peacock.
Having stolen red garments, a jivajivaka; having stolen pigments and perfumes here, a man
gets musk-rat-hood; the Brahmin intent on greed lives there for fifteen years.
Having exhausted unrighteousness, he is then born a human. Having stolen milk, a crane is born.
The man who in delusion steals oil, he too, Brahmins, dying, is born an oil-drinker (cockroach).
The lowest of men who, armed, kills an unarmed man for wealth or as an enemy, dying is born an ass.
The ass lives two years, then is killed by weapon; dead, he is born in a deer's womb, constantly afraid.
A year having passed, the deer is pierced by a weapon; the deer killed is then a fish, and he too is caught in a net.
When the fourth month arrives, he is born a beast of prey; a beast of prey ten years, a leopard five years;
then, reaching death, driven by the cycle of time, having exhausted his unrighteousness, he attains human-hood.
Having stolen an instrument, a man is born a hairy one; likewise the man who steals food mixed with oil-cake
is born a brown-maned fierce mouse, always biting humans, a sinner, best of Brahmins.
Having stolen ghee, the evil-minded is born a crow or diver; having stolen fish or meat, he is born a crow.
Having stolen salt he is born a cirikaka; the man who denies a deposit made in trust
is deprived of life, and by that is born in a fish's womb; having attained a fish's womb, dying he is born a human.
Having attained human-hood he is born short-lived; a man having committed sins is born an animal, Brahmins.
He does not know dharma by his own measure at all, those men who, having committed sins, always cast them off by vows.
Joined with pleasure and pain, they become sick; they are born unclothed, and even as barbarians, no doubt.
Men of sinful conduct, joined with greed and delusion, but men who avoid sins from birth
become healthy, handsome and wealthy; women too by this arrangement, having done sin, obtain (its result).
They become wives of these same sinners; the faults in stealing are mostly all so declared.
This has been told to you in outline, best of Brahmins; in another connection of narrative you will hear more, Brahmins.
This, fortunate ones, was heard by me from Brahma when he spoke in the midst of gods and sages, and when asked as well.
It has been narrated by me to you completely and duly; hearing it, best of sages, set your mind on dharma.
A man, though having done what ought not to be done, is then joined with dharma; of all gifts, food is declared the best.
All food should be given, by one wishing dharma, in uprightness; for life-breaths of men are food, and from food a creature is born.
The worlds rest on food, therefore food is praised; gods, sages, ancestors and humans praise food alone.
By giving food a man attains heaven; excellent food justly obtained should be given to the twice-born.
With glad inner self to those endowed with Vedic study — he whose food ten Brahmins eat even once,
given with a glad mind, would not go to an animal state. By feeding ten thousand Brahmins, best of Brahmins,
a man ever fond of sin is freed from unrighteousness. A Brahmin with the Veda in front, having gathered food by begging,
giving it here to a Brahmin devoted to Vedic study, prospers happily; without harming Brahmins' property and protecting it justly,
the Kshatriya who gives to Brahmins, chiefs in the Veda, with purity and composure food gained by his strength,
by that the righteous-souled one removes his evil action, Brahmins; and the share of agriculture earned, purified of the sixth part,
the Vaishya giving to the twice-born is freed from sins; food gained with hardship and risk of life,
the Shudra giving food to the twice-born is freed from sin; even a harming person who has earned food by his own power
and gives it to Brahmins does not go to hard places. The man who with joy gives to Vedic elders among Brahmins food justly obtained
is freed from sin. Food is vigour-giving in the world; having given it, the man becomes vigorous.
Having followed the path of the good, he is freed from all sins; the path made by the knowers of giving, by which the wise go —
among them too the givers of food have eternal dharma for them. Food justly obtained by a man in every circumstance
should always be given; food is the supreme goal. By giving food a man goes to the supreme goal.
Joined with all desires, after death he enjoys happiness; thus, joined with merit, a man is freed from sins.
Therefore food free of injustice should be given. A householder who always eats after the offering to the life-breaths,
should make the day fruitful by giving food; a man who feeds a hundred of the best Veda-knowers constantly,
knowers of justice, knowers of dharma and of the Itihasa, does not go to fearful hell nor serve rebirth.
Joined with all desires, after death he enjoys happiness; thus joined with action, he rejoices free of fever.
He is born handsome, famous and wealthy. This great fruit of food-giving has been told to you all; it is the root of dharmas and of gifts, Brahmins.
By reciting your name the night-roamers flee, beings run away and enemies depart; destruction now comes to them, Vishnu; dharma and truth become supreme here.
Thus praised by the ancestors, the supporter of the earth, pleased, then manifested his divine form; at Kokamukha the god saw the host of ancestors immersed in water, bearing a rock on their heads.
Seeing them sunk in water, Janardana in boar form resolved to lift the frightened host of ancestors.
Striking the rock with the tip of his tusk, the boar flung it and the lord lifted the ancestors from the rock's surface.
The ancestors, clinging to the Varaha's tusk, golden and radiant, were made fearless at Kokamukha by the god Vishnu.
Having lifted the ancestors, the god, the boar, at Vishnu-tirtha, Vishnu concentrated and gave water to them at Loharagala.
Then Keshava took kusha grass born from his own hair, sesame born of his sweat, and made an excellent firebrand,
made the light shining like the sun a vessel, and the wished-for holy place, and stood beneath Koti-vata, with pure water held by Ganga.
From the peak Tunga taking the juices of sacrificial herbs, honey and milk juices, perfumes, flowers, incense and unguents,
taking a cow from the lake, taking jewels from the ocean, marking the earth with his tusk and sprinkling it with water,
plastering it with what arose from his heat, marking it again with kusha, circumambulating it with a firebrand and repeatedly sprinkling it,
taking kusha pointing east, he called the sages standing in the pores of his hair and asked: "I shall do the libation to ancestors."
When they said "Do so," the lord then called the Vishvedevas by mantra and gave them seats.
Hari, bearer of discus and mace, calling them by mantra with the Vedic procedure, made protection of the deities with unbroken rice grains.
The akshatas (unbroken grains), barley and herbs, born of portions of all the gods, protect everywhere the directions; they were made for protection.
Among gods, Danavas, Daityas, Yakshas and Rakshasas, none in the moving and unmoving world is able to harm them.
Since they were made by none, therefore they are akshata; they were appointed by Vishnu formerly for the protection of the gods.
The boar, making arghya with kusha, perfume, barley and flowers, "To the Vishvedevas," then asked them:
I shall invoke the ancestors, divine and human. Told "Invoke," the pure one invoked.
The knower of the Veda gave the kusha with joined roots and tips, with sesame, placing his hand on his knee, and a seat with the left.
Likewise with one hand on the knee, Varaha, saying "Let the ancestors and Brahmins come to us,"
said "Apahata," and made protection by the left, and made the invocation of the ancestors by name and gotra.
Saying "Ancestors, come swift as thought," reciting "through the years," he then placed the arghya on them.
The immortal speeches that stand, what is mine of father's father, my grandfathers — thus he gave the arghya to the grandfather.
